title: Rerum Novarum again (1891)
hook: a worker signs for a wage too low to live on: is the deal fair because it was agreed?

segments.voice: Yesterday, care for creation: Brother Sun, Sister Water. Your line was our common home. Did a tap remind you of someone downstream? Day one thousand three hundred.

Back to Leo's letter, the one this block opened with. Its closing line says it was given at Rome in 1891. Today, one question inside it, the kind that lands every payday. A worker needs a job. There's no other job in sight. The owner offers a wage too small to live on, and the worker signs. Hands are shaken. Nobody was forced at gunpoint. So is that wage fair, simply because both sides agreed to it? Plenty of arguments say a deal is a deal. Leo's letter says something else. Today, a just wage.
screen: `BACK TO LEO'S LETTER.` → `NO OTHER JOB IN SIGHT.` → `IS A DEAL ALWAYS FAIR?`

segments.voice: First, Leo's answer. He writes that when a worker accepts harder terms because necessity, or fear of something worse, leaves no choice, the worker is the victim of force and injustice. A signature made with no real alternative doesn't make a wage just. Second, the measure. Leo says a wage must be enough to support a worker who lives frugally and behaves well. And he hopes for more: a wage that lets a worker support a wife and children in reasonable comfort, and still put a little aside, so that over time ordinary workers might come to own something themselves. Third, the roots in scripture. Sending out disciples in Luke, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "the labourer is worthy of his hire." The Greek word for hire there is misthos, wages. And the letter of James warns the rich that the wages held back from the workers who reaped their fields cry out, and that the cry reaches the ears of the Lord. Leo's letter stands in that line. Fourth, what it means now. The Catechism calls a just wage the legitimate fruit of work, and says that refusing or withholding it can be a grave injustice. Today people speak of a living wage, which is close to what Leo described. What counts as enough changes with the place and the prices. The principle stays put: in this teaching, honest work should pay enough to live on and to raise a family.
screen: `A DEAL ISN'T ENOUGH.` · `ENOUGH FOR A FAMILY.` · then, large: `WORTHY OF HIS HIRE.` · then: `THE LEGITIMATE FRUIT OF WORK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn what a living wage is where you live. After the bell, if you like, look it up: what a household in your town needs to cover rent, food and the basics. For now, settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone whose work your day depends on. The person who stocks the shelves. The aide at a care home. The cook. Ask, without rushing to an answer: could their pay support a family here? Just hold the question. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
Just wage. In Leo's letter, a wage enough for a worker to live on and support a family, and not made just merely because it was agreed. Today's word.
Your line: a just wage. Today, find out one number: what it actually costs to live where you do, and hold it next to the pay of someone who serves you. Day one thousand three hundred.

howItsDone: Catholic bishops and organizations cite Rerum Novarum in debates about minimum and living wages, and Catholic employers are urged by Church teaching to pay wages that let workers support a family.

notes: The year 1891 is stated in the hook on the authority of Rerum Novarum's closing line ('Given at St. Peter's in Rome, the fifteenth day of May, 1891'); confirm. The title keeps the index's '(1891)'.

Rerum Novarum 45 paraphrased: wages must not be insufficient to support a frugal and well-behaved wage-earner; a worker who accepts harder conditions through necessity or fear of a worse evil is 'the victim of force and injustice'. RN 46 paraphrased: a wage enabling a worker to support wife and children and to save, so that more might become owners. Paragraph numbers vary between editions.
CCC 2434 paraphrased ('a just wage is the legitimate fruit of work'; refusing or withholding it 'can be a grave injustice').
'Plenty of arguments say a deal is a deal' is a general framing, not a claim about any school of thought; confirm it is fair.

Editor: cut a line echoing day 1292 ('carried it onto the factory floor'); removed the unsourced 'a full week of work' standard and tied the principle to the teaching; the practice no longer assumes the listener has a parent in care.
